sources.text: --- title: Fueter regularity and discrete series description: Weighted regular spinors, explicit group actions, compact types, and proofs of irreducibility and square-integrability. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: exposition order: 4 --- # Fueter regularity and discrete series :::discussion Fueter regularity realizes an entire family of discrete-series representations when the coefficients are compatible symmetric spinors. The construction below gives the Hilbert spaces, the group action, and the proofs. The case of one unrestricted quaternionic value is the Hardy limit discussed in the following article. ::: ## The group and its coefficient spaces Put $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$, $K=\operatorname{Sp}(1)_L\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)_R$, $B=\{q\in\mathbb H:|q|<1\}$, and $s(q)=1-|q|^2$. Explicitly $G=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb H):g^*\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)g=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\}$, where $g^*$ is conjugate transpose. Its action is $gq=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1}$ and $K$ consists of $\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$ with $|a|=|b|=1$. All representations and Hilbert spaces below are complex. For quaternion coefficients, the complex scalar acts on the right. Let $V_n=\mathbb C[X,Y]_n$ with $$ (\tau_n(M)p)(X,Y)=p(aX+cY,bX+dY),\qquad M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}, $$ and the norm $$ \left\|\sum_{k=0}^n c_kX^{n-k}Y^k\right\|_n^2 =\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{|c_k|^2}{\binom nk}. $$ A quaternion acts through $$ \iota(t+ix+jy+kz)=\begin{pmatrix}t+ix&y+iz\\-y+iz&t-ix\end{pmatrix}. $$ Write a quaternion-valued homogeneous polynomial of auxiliary degree $n-1$ as $$ h(q;X,Y)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h_k(q)X^{n-1-k}Y^k=A(q;X,Y)-jB(q;X,Y), $$ where $A,B$ have complex coefficients. Auxiliary variables commute with quaternion coefficients. For $n\ge1$, put $$ W_n=\{A-jB:A_Y=B_X\}\subset\mathbb H[X,Y]_{n-1}. \tag{C1} $$ Here $A,B\in\mathbb C[X,Y]_{n-1}$; we refer to $A_Y=B_X$ as the compatibility condition. The first compact factor acts trivially on $V_n$. Let $T_np=p_X-jp_Y$ and $\mathcal T_n=T_n/n$ for $n\ge1$. For a quaternion coefficient row of length $n$, use the squared norm $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|h_k|^2/\binom{n-1}{k}$; the auxiliary variables $X,Y$ commute with coefficients. Write $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$, coefficientwise, with $x=x_1,y=x_2,z=x_3$ in the foundations article. The compatibility condition is imposed pointwise for functions of $q$. Proposition [DS1](#ds1) identifies $W_n$ with $V_n$ and proves that its complex dimension is $n+1$. ::::proposition DS1 | The spinor-to-Fueter isometry Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $n\ge1$, $\mathcal T_n:V_n\to W_n$ is a complex-linear isometric isomorphism, with inverse $A-jB\mapsto XA+YB$. In particular $\dim_{\mathbb C}W_n=n+1$. :::proof Proof of DS1 The polynomials $f_X/n$ and $f_Y/n$ satisfy the compatibility condition, and for $h=A-jB\in W_n$ the inverse is particularly simple: $$ \mathcal T_n^{-1}h=XA+YB. \tag{C5} $$ Differentiating (C5), using $A_Y=B_X$ and Euler's identity, gives $(XA+YB)_X=nA$ and $(XA+YB)_Y=nB$. This proves the inverse formula. For a monomial $X^{n-k}Y^k$, the squared norm of $T_n$'s image is $$ \frac{(n-k)^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}}+ \frac{k^2}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}} =\frac{n^2}{\binom nk}, $$ with absent endpoint terms omitted. Images of distinct monomials are orthogonal for the underlying complex inner product, proving the isometry. ::: :::: ## Weighted Hilbert spaces and the action Use Euclidean volume $dv=dt\,dx\,dy\,dz$ on $B$. ::::definition DS-D2 | Weighted Regular Functions Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1), [DS1](#ds1). --- For an integer $n\ge2$, put $C_n=n(n-1)/\pi^2$. The **weighted regular space** consists of the smooth functions in $$ \mathcal H_n=\left\{h:B\longrightarrow W_n: D_lh=0,\quad \|h\|_{\mathcal H_n}^2 =C_n\int_B\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{|h_k(q)|^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}} s(q)^{n-2}\,dv(q)<\infty\right\}, \tag{C2} $$ where $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$ acts coefficientwise. :::: The polynomial-spinor model is $$ \mathcal B_n=\{f\in L^2(B,V_n,d\mu_n):D_l(T_nf)=0\},\quad d\mu_n=C_ns^{n-2}dv.\tag{C6} $$ Here the equation is imposed distributionally. The map $\mathcal T_n$ identifies $\mathcal B_n$ isometrically with $\mathcal H_n$ by [DS1](#ds1); smoothness of the distributional kernels is proved in [DS2](#ds2). The measure $\mu_n$ has total mass one, since polar coordinates give $$ \int_Bs^{n-2}dv =2\pi^2\int_0^1r^3(1-r^2)^{n-2}\,dr =\frac{\pi^2}{n(n-1)}. $$ For $\gamma\in G$, write $$ \gamma^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad q'=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1},\qquad J=cq+d. $$ Let $S_m(M)$ be the coefficient-column matrix of $\tau_m(M)$ in descending monomials; in particular $S_1(M)=M$. Regard $h=(h_0,\ldots,h_{n-1})$ as a row. ::::construction DS-C1 | The Möbius Representation Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1), [DS-D2](#ds-d2). Justification: The group law, covariance, and unitarity in [DS2](#ds2). Origin: consequence --- Define $$ \boxed{(\Pi_n(\gamma)h)(q) =|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q')\,S_{n-1}(\iota(J^{-1}))^t.} \tag{C3} $$ The matrix entries multiply quaternion coefficients on the right, while $J^{-1}$ multiplies on the left. On polynomial spinors the corresponding formula is $$ (\pi_n(\gamma)f)(q)=|J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})f(q').\tag{C7} $$ :::: ::::theorem DS2 | Completeness, covariance, and unitarity Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS-D2](#ds-d2), [DS-C1](#ds-c1), [SC3](spinor-connection.md#sc3). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For $n\ge2$, $\mathcal H_n$ and $\mathcal B_n$ are nonzero complete Hilbert spaces. Their distributional kernels have smooth harmonic representatives. The formulas in DS-C1 define strongly continuous unitary group representations, and $\mathcal T_n\pi_n=\Pi_n\mathcal T_n$. :::proof Proof of DS2 The Schmid-kernel realization is [[1, eq. (2.8), Prop. 3.6]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012); [SC3](spinor-connection.md#sc3) gives its expression in the present frame. If $D_l(T_nf)=0$ distributionally, apply $\overline D_l=\partial_t-i\partial_x-j\partial_y-k\partial_z$. Since $\overline D_lD_l=\Delta$ and $T_n$ is a fixed injective linear map, $\Delta f=0$ distributionally. Weyl's lemma gives a smooth harmonic representative. In particular all its coefficient functions are harmonic. For a convergent sequence in the weighted $L^2$ norm, convergence also holds in $L^2$ on each compact subset, because the weight is strictly positive there. The distributional equation passes to the limit, as does the fixed algebraic fibre constraint. Consequently (C6) is closed and complete. Interior harmonic estimates make evaluation at each point continuous. This also justifies differentiating and averaging its vectors inside the ball. Quaternion arguments of $\tau_n$ always mean their $\iota$ matrices. The cocycle $J(g_1g_2,q)=J(g_1,g_2q)J(g_2,q)$ proves the group law with the indicated inverse-element convention. The polynomial chain rule shows $$ \mathcal T_n\pi_n(\gamma)=\Pi_n(\gamma)\mathcal T_n, $$ including the inverse and transpose in (C3). For covariance of the differential equation, lift $f$ to $$ F_f(g)=|d|^{-2}\tau_n(d^{-1})f(g\cdot0),\qquad g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}. \tag{C8} $$ Here the blocks belong to $g$, not its inverse. This is a right-K-equivariant function, $F_f(gk)=\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}F_f(g)$. The [connection and weight theorem](spinor-connection.md#sc3) establishes $$ 24(\mathscr DF_f)(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+4)/2}D_l(T_nf),\qquad F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q). \tag{C9} $$ Left translation on the lifted space commutes with $\mathscr D$, so it preserves the kernel and gives (C7). The connection and its curvature are included in that calculation. For unitarity, write $r=|J|$. Then $$ s(q')=s(q)/r^2,\qquad dv(q')=r^{-8}dv(q),\qquad \||J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})v\|^2=r^{-2n-4}\|v\|^2. $$ These factors cancel exactly against the weight $s^{n-2}$ in the change of variables. Hence (C7), and therefore (C3), are unitary. Strong continuity follows first on compactly supported continuous functions in the ambient weighted $L^2$ space by change of variables, then by density and unitarity; the closed invariant kernel inherits it. Nonzeroness follows from the constant $V_n$-valued functions. ::: :::: ## Irreducibility and discrete series ::::theorem DS3 | Irreducibility by compact averaging Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For each $n\ge2$, the representation on $\mathcal B_n$, equivalently on $\mathcal H_n$, is irreducible. The group translates of the constant $V_n$ have dense span. :::proof Proof of DS3 The compact action is $$ (\pi_n(a,b)f)(q)=\tau_n(b)f(a^{-1}qb). \tag{C10} $$ Average over the first factor, with Haar probability measure: $$ (P_Lf)(q)=\int_{\operatorname{Sp}(1)}f(a^{-1}q)\,da=f(0). \tag{C11} $$ For $q\ne0$, this is the spherical mean of the harmonic function $f$ over the sphere of radius $|q|$; for $q=0$ it is immediate. Thus $P_L$ is the orthogonal projection onto the constant $V_n$. The second compact factor acts irreducibly on those constants by $\tau_n$. Let $M$ be a nonzero closed $G$-invariant subspace. Choose $f\in M$ and a point $p$ with $f(p)\ne0$. Transitivity and the invertible fibre multiplier give a translate $\pi_n(g)f$ nonzero at $0$. Averaging that vector by $P_L$ gives a nonzero constant in $M$. Its second-compact-factor orbit spans the entire constant $V_n$, so $M$ contains every constant. If $M$ were proper, unitarity would make $M^\perp$ another nonzero closed invariant subspace. The same argument would put all constants in $M^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore the representation is irreducible. Equivalently, the translates of its constant $V_n$ span a dense subspace. ::: :::: ::::theorem DS4 | A closed embedding into the regular representation Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2), [DS3](#ds3). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For $n\ge2$, the representation belongs to the discrete series of $\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$. For any nonzero $v\in V_n$, let $c_v$ be its constant function and put $(\mathcal W_vf)(g)=\langle\pi_n(g^{-1})f,c_v\rangle$, with inner product linear in the first argument. This map has closed image in $L^2(G)$ and satisfies $$ \|\mathcal W_vf\|_{L^2(G)}^2=\frac{\|v\|^2}{(n+1)C_n}\|f\|_{\mathcal B_n}^2 $$ for the Haar measure specified in the proof. :::proof Proof of DS4 Fix Haar measure by $$ \int_G\Phi(g)\,dg=\int_B\int_K\Phi(\sigma(q)k)\,dk\,s(q)^{-4}dv(q), \qquad \int_Kdk=1 $$ in this disintegration convention. The base measure is invariant. Let $v\in V_n$ be nonzero and $c_v$ its constant function. Use a complex inner product linear in the first argument. Harmonic mean values and the probability measure give $$ \langle f,c_v\rangle_{\mathcal B_n}=\langle f(0),v\rangle_{V_n}. $$ The matrix-coefficient map $$ (\mathcal W_vf)(g) =\langle\pi_n(g^{-1})f,c_v\rangle =\langle F_f(g),v\rangle \tag{C12} $$ intertwines $\pi_n$ with left translation on functions on $G$. Schur orthogonality for the finite-dimensional irreducible $\tau_n$ gives $$ \int_K|\langle\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}u,v\rangle|^2dk =\frac{\|u\|^2\|v\|^2}{n+1}. $$ Since $F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q)$, we obtain the exact norm identity $$ \boxed{\|\mathcal W_vf\|_{L^2(G)}^2 =\frac{\|v\|^2}{(n+1)C_n}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_n}^2.} \tag{C13} $$ Thus a fixed scalar multiple of $\mathcal W_v$ is an isometric embedding with closed invariant image in $L^2(G)$. Together with irreducibility, this proves that $\mathcal B_n$ and $\mathcal H_n$ are discrete series. For normalized $v$, the inverse constant in (C13) is $n(n^2-1)/\pi^2$ for the specified Haar measure. Its vanishing at the endpoint is consistent with the divergence proved in [H4](fueter-hardy-space.md#h4); it is not used as a substitute for that argument. ::: :::: ## Compact types and explicit vectors ::::theorem DS5 | The complete compact decomposition Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2), Clebsch–Gordan and spherical harmonic decomposition. Review: pending Formal: none Origin: literature Cite: [[1, Thms. 3.9, 3.11]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012) --- For $n\ge2$, $$ \mathcal H_n|_K\simeq\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m\ge0}V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n}. $$ Every type occurs once. Coordinate degree $m$ has dimension $(m+1)(m+n+1)$, and the constants form the unique minimal type $V_0\boxtimes V_n$. The same polynomial-kernel calculation holds for $n=1$ and supplies the compact types of the Hardy space. :::proof Proof of DS5 Let $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ be the degree-$m$ homogeneous polynomials in the real coordinates of $q$, valued in $V_n$, satisfying $D_l(T_nf)=0$. Harmonicity puts this space inside $$ \mathrm{SH}_m(\mathbb R^4)\otimes V_n \simeq V_m\boxtimes(V_m\otimes V_n). $$ Here the scalar spherical harmonics on $S^3\simeq\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ carry the standard left/right type $V_m\boxtimes V_m$. For the right factor set $R_jf=\partial_{qe_j}f$, where $e_0=1,e_1=i,e_2=j,e_3=k$. On degree-$m$ functions $R_0=mI$. The infinitesimal action is $d\tau_n(e_j)+R_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, so its Casimir is $$ C_R=-n(n+2)-m(m+2)+2\sum_{j=1}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_j. $$ The equation forces the cross term to be $-mn$. To check this without an implicit coordinate change, put $\mathbf Tf=(f_X,f_Y)^t$ and write the flat equation as $$ \sum_{i=0}^3\iota(e_i)\mathbf T(\partial_if)=0. $$ Multiply on the left by $\iota(\bar q)$ and contract a column $(A,B)^t$ to $XA+YB$. The result is $$ 0=\sum_i d\tau_n(\bar qe_i)\partial_if =\sum_{j=0}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_jf. \tag{C14} $$ The last equality follows from $\bar qe_i=\sum_j\langle qe_j,e_i\rangle e_j$. The $j=0$ term is $nmf$, proving the assertion. Consequently $C_R$ acts as $$ -(m+n)(m+n+2). $$ The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of $V_m\otimes V_n$ has distinct Casimir values and contains $V_{m+n}$ once. Hence $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ lies in $V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n}$. It is nonzero: the explicit seed $$ f_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^n \tag{C15} $$ is regular, because $(\partial_t+i\partial_x)(t+ix)^m=0$. Since the candidate compact summand is irreducible and the kernel is $K$-invariant, its nonzero subspace is the whole summand. Thus $$ \mathcal P_{m,n}=V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n},\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}\mathcal P_{m,n}=(m+1)(m+n+1). $$ Harmonic functions on the ball have homogeneous harmonic expansions. Their degrees are orthogonal on every sphere, and therefore for the radial measure $d\mu_n$. The flat first-order equation holds separately on each homogeneous term. Parseval's identity on spheres and integration in the radius show that partial sums converge in the Hilbert norm. This proves the complete direct-sum decomposition in the theorem. ::: :::: ::::proposition DS6 | Polynomial seeds and translated constants Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS3](#ds3), [DS5](#ds5). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $n\ge2$ and $m\ge0$, the vectors $h_m=(t+ix)^mX^{n-1}$ span each compact type under $K$, have squared norm $m!/(n+1)_m$, and the translates of constant spinors displayed in the proof have dense span. :::proof Proof of DS6 Under $\mathcal T_n$, the seed becomes the particularly simple quaternion-valued polynomial $$ h_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^{n-1}. $$ Its squared norm is $$ \|h_m\|^2=\frac{m!}{(n+1)_m},\qquad (n+1)_m=(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+m), \tag{C16} $$ by the beta integral. Its $K$-orbit spans the entire type of degree $m$. Constants ($m=0$) are the minimal type; the two highest-weight labels increase with $m$, also making this the unique minimum for the usual compact highest-weight norm. An additional supply of nonpolynomial examples comes directly from translated constants. For any $p\in B$ and $v\in V_n$, $$ f_{p,v}(q)=s(p)^{(n+2)/2}|1-\bar pq|^{-2} \tau_n((1-\bar pq)^{-1})v =\pi_n(\sigma(p))c_v(q). \tag{C17} $$ These are regular spinors of norm $\|v\|$, and $\mathcal T_nf_{p,v}$ are corresponding Fueter-regular vectors. Their span is dense by DS3. For the norm, put $u=t^2+x^2$ and $v=y^2+z^2$. Euclidean measure becomes $\pi^2du\,dv$ after angular integration, so $$ C_n\pi^2\int_{u+v<1}u^m(1-u-v)^{n-2}du\,dv =\frac{m!\,n!}{(m+n)!}. $$ For a translate, $\sigma(p)^{-1}$ has $c=-\bar p/\sqrt{s(p)}$ and $d=1/\sqrt{s(p)}$; substituting these blocks in C7 gives the displayed formula, and unitarity gives its norm. ::: :::: ::::corollary DS7 | The first member as a pair of regular functions Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS2](#ds2), [DS5](#ds5), [DS6](#ds6). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- The $n=2$ representation is the space of pairs $(h_0,h_1)=(a-jb,b-jc)$, with $a,b,c$ complex functions on $B$, satisfying coefficientwise Fueter regularity and $$ \|h\|^2=\frac2{\pi^2}\int_B(|h_0|^2+|h_1|^2)\,dv<\infty. $$ Its minimal compact type has complex dimension three. :::proof Proof of DS7 For $n=2$, write $$ f=a(q)X^2+2b(q)XY+c(q)Y^2,\qquad h=\mathcal T_2f=(a-jb)X+(b-jc)Y, $$ where $a,b,c$ are complex-valued. Thus the representation consists exactly of pairs $$ (h_0,h_1)=(a-jb,\ b-jc) $$ that are componentwise Fueter-regular and satisfy $$ \|h\|^2=\frac2{\pi^2}\int_B(|h_0|^2+|h_1|^2)\,dv<\infty. $$ The measure is ordinary ball volume, up to normalization. The action is fully explicit: $$ (\Pi_2(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}(h_0(q'),h_1(q'))\iota(J^{-1})^t. $$ Constant pairs of this form constitute the three-dimensional complex minimal $K$-type. The pair $(t+ix,0)$ is a nonconstant vector, of squared norm $1/3$, in the next compact type of complex dimension $8$. All formulas follow by inserting $n=2$ into the preceding definitions and theorems. ::: :::: :::discussion This is the $l=n$, quaternionic-dimension-one family in [[1]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012), §§2–3. The compact-type calculation follows their Theorem 3.9; DS3–DS4 give direct arguments for irreducibility and square-integrability. The ordinary quaternion-valued endpoint is developed in [The Fueter Hardy space](fueter-hardy-space.md), and the section calculation is in [Connections and the Fueter equation](spinor-connection.md). The local [closed pairings](regular-differential-forms.md) lead to separate quotient questions. ::: ## References 1. Heping Liu and Genkai Zhang, [*Realization of quaternionic discrete series on the unit ball in Hᵈ*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfa.2011.12.019), Journal of Functional Analysis **262** (2012), 2979–3005.

## 2. An isometric passage to polynomial spinors

Define
$$
\mathcal T_n:V_n\longrightarrow W_n,\qquad
\mathcal T_nf=\frac1n(f_X-jf_Y).
\tag{C4}
$$
This differs from the earlier $T_n$ by the scalar $1/n$, so that it is an isometry. Indeed $f_X/n$ and $f_Y/n$ satisfy the compatibility condition, and for $h=A-jB\in W_n$ the inverse is particularly simple:
$$
\mathcal T_n^{-1}h=XA+YB.
\tag{C5}
$$
Differentiating (C5) and using $A_Y=B_X$ and Euler's identity proves (C4). For a monomial $X^{n-k}Y^k$, the squared norm of $T_n$'s image is
$$
\frac{(n-k)^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}}+
\frac{k^2}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}
=\frac{n^2}{\binom nk},
$$
with absent endpoint terms omitted. Images of distinct monomials are orthogonal for the underlying complex inner product, proving the isometry.
